title: The Gods and the Blade of Grass
hookLine: the gods brag about a victory, and a single blade of grass won't burn: ahamkara
carry: ahamkara, the I-maker, claims what it didn't do
tomorrow: Krishna calls the body a field

cards: The Kena Upanishad tells it. The gods win a great battle, and they celebrate: our victory, our greatness. Then a strange being appears before them, and no one can say what it is.
Agni, the god of fire, goes to find out. Who are you? it asks. I'm Agni.
I can burn up everything on earth. The being sets down a single blade of grass. Burn this.
Agni rushes at it with all his force, and can't. Vayu, the wind, tries next: I can carry off anything on earth. The grass doesn't move.

teach.b: Samkhya has a precise name for the gods' mistake, and puts it in a surprising place. The Samkhya Karika lays out the order of unfolding. From prakriti, the root, comes mahat, the great one, also called buddhi.
Buddhi is marked by deciding: this, not that.
From buddhi comes ahamkara, marked by the claim of I. Translators often render it ego, or the I-maker. It's the reflex that says our victory, my idea, my turn, before anyone checks.
Notice the order: in Samkhya, deciding and the sense of me unfold before earth and water.
And notice the side of the line. Buddhi and ahamkara both belong to prakriti. They're instruments, finely made, but not purusha, the witness.
The Bhagavad Gita puts it in one line: all actions are done by the gunas of prakriti, but the one confused by ahamkara thinks, I am the doer. Hindus act on that teaching every day.
After a puja, a meal or a day's work, many say a short line that hands it over: Krishnarpanam, to Krishna; and at the sacred fire, idam na mama, this is not mine.
Hindu schools explain the self in different ways, and they'll have their say. But in Samkhya, the I-maker is a tool, and tools can be noticed.
Today, when something goes well, ask the question Uma answered for Indra: whose victory is it?

how: Students of Samkhya, and of the Yoga traditions that use its map, learn the unfolding of prakriti in order, from buddhi and ahamkara down to the elements. Many Hindus close a puja or a day's work by offering it to God, often with words like Sri Krishnarpanamastu.

o: a teaching that the mind is made of pure light
a school where even the sense of I is part of nature
a school that teaches the ego is evil and sinful

p: the great one, also called buddhi
marked by the claim of I

s: in Samkhya, ahamkara is the true self
ahamkara belongs to prakriti. the witness is purusha.
in the Kena Upanishad, the gods learn the victory was Brahman's
Uma tells Indra: the victory was Brahman's, and you were boasting.
in Samkhya, the elements come first and the mind last
the order runs from the inside out: buddhi, then the I, then senses and elements.

games.q: your team wins, and everyone posts "we did this." by the Kena story and the Gita, what fits?
o: enjoy it, and remember it came through you, not only from you.
never celebrate anything; all joy is ahamkara.
take all the credit; you earned every bit.
games.why: the gods weren't wrong to win; they were wrong to say ours. the Gita: the gunas act, and ahamkara says, I am the doer.

practice: Think of one thing that went well this week: a grade, a meal, a kind word. Notice how fast the tag arrives: I did that.

Then trace it outward: the teacher who explained, the hands that grew the food, the breath that came on its own. If you pray, close by offering it, the way many Hindus do: Krishnarpanam, or the name of God you use.
If you don't, just say quietly: not only mine.

wordCard.voice: Samkhya. Its map unfolds from the root: first buddhi, which decides, then ahamkara, which says I. Both on nature's side of the line.

orig.note: Sanskrit: in Samkhya, the principle marked by the claim of I, unfolding from buddhi; often translated ego.

carryVoice: Your line: ahamkara, the I-maker, claims what it didn't do. The grass didn't burn. I'll be here tomorrow.

sources.ref: Kena Upanishad 3.1–4.1 (the gods' victory; the wondrous being; Agni and Vayu fail at a blade of grass; Uma Haimavati tells Indra it was Brahman)
Samkhya Karika 22 (from prakriti, mahat; from it, ahamkara; from that, the group of sixteen)
Samkhya Karika 24 (ahamkara marked by self-assertion, the claim of I)
Bhagavad Gita 3.27 (actions are done by the gunas; deluded by ahamkara, one thinks 'I am the doer')
